value.overview: The White-tailed Hawk (Geranoaetus albicaudatus) is a large, broad-winged raptor of open country in the tropical and subtropical Americas. It often hunts while soaring or hovering over grasslands, savannas, dry scrub, and agricultural landscapes. Adults are mainly slate gray above and white below, with reddish shoulders and a conspicuous white tail crossed by a black band. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident, especially in the northwestern lowlands.
value.classification: The White-tailed Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and family Accipitridae. It is closely related to other large soaring hawks and was formerly often placed in the genus Buteo.
value.identification: Adults have long, broad wings, a slate-gray back, reddish or chestnut shoulders, white underparts, and a white tail with a bold black subterminal band. The wings extend noticeably beyond the tail when the bird is perched. Immatures are browner and more heavily marked, with a less sharply defined tail pattern. In flight, the species may hold its wings slightly bent at the shoulders while soaring. The tail pattern helps separate it from Short-tailed Hawk and Harris’s Hawk.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and much of South America to central Argentina. It favors open habitats such as grasslands, savannas, dry forest edges, scrub, pastures, cultivated areas, and plains with scattered trees or shrubs. In Costa Rica it is a very uncommon resident, concentrated mainly in the lowlands and foothills of Guanacaste, particularly near the Cordillera de Guanacaste. Older records came from parts of the central highlands, and possible residence has also been suggested for the Térraba savannas.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and not considered a regular long-distance migrant there. The Costa Rican official bird list classifies it as a resident species, although movements may occur locally or seasonally in response to food and weather.
value.breeding: White-tailed Hawks build a substantial platform nest from sticks, sometimes adding leaves and other plant material. The nest is usually placed high in a tree in open savanna or similar habitat. Two white or lightly brown-marked eggs are commonly reported. In Costa Rica, a nest near Taboga in Guanacaste was observed in February with two downy young, supporting local breeding. Nesting sites are typically surrounded by open ground that provides access to hunting areas.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is varied and consists mainly of small to medium-sized mammals, including rodents, along with reptiles, birds, large insects, and other available prey. The hawk commonly searches from soaring flight, hovering or kiting over open ground, and perches on trees, shrubs, poles, or other elevated lookouts. It may also exploit prey fleeing grass or brush fires, a behavior recorded in grassland habitats.
value.behavior: This hawk is usually seen alone or in pairs, soaring over open landscapes on rising air currents. It often remains nearly stationary while facing into the wind and scanning the ground below. When not hunting, it perches conspicuously on isolated trees, shrubs, fence posts, or utility poles. Adults may defend breeding territories, and other small birds sometimes nest near its nest, apparently gaining some protection from predators.

conservation.populationTrend: Stable or possibly increasing overall, although reliable long-term information is limited in parts of its range.
